title: MetaPerch: Learning from metadata for bioacoustics foundation models
claim: Models trained on one data source face domain shifts at evaluation, in both input conditions and target classes, which auxiliary signals could bridge.
layout: 2 panels split by dashed line, training left, evaluation right, double arrows crossing
description: The figure is split by a vertical dashed line into Training (left) and Evaluation (right). The Training side shows logos of four data sources (XC, iNat, FSD50K, Tiersimmen) above a large spectrogram of a focal bird recording. Below it, under the label Metadata, is a row of six icons: location pin, calendar, clock, text note, waveform and microphone. The Evaluation side lists BirdSet, BEANS and WABAD above two stacked spectrograms. The upper one is labeled Novel Species and the lower one Soundscapes. Two large yellow double-headed arrows cross the divider. Species Shift runs horizontally to the upper spectrogram. Acoustic Shift runs diagonally to the lower spectrogram. The eye goes first to the large headings and the yellow arrows.
caption: Problem setup. Bioacoustics training and evaluation settings differ significantly. This figure illustrates substantial acoustic (focal →soundscape) and species (observed →novel) domain shifts in our setup. In this work, we explore the use of metadata as auxiliary supervision to learn robust, generalizable features and help bridge the domain gap.
abstract: Bioacoustic foundation models rely on large-scale citizen science platforms like Xeno-Canto for geographically and ecologically diverse data. Recent work has shown that supervision alone can produce SotA species detection models when trained on this large-scale data -- however, there remains unutilized potential in the form of recording metadata readily available within these community-driven data hubs. In this work, we explore the use of metadata -- such as location and time -- as auxiliary supervision signals, allowing the model to leverage species-metadata correlations in its learned representation. Auxiliary metadata losses provide additional information beyond vocalizations alone that can encourage a richer, more robust representation that generalizes better to species distribution and acoustic domain shifts -- important challenges for deployment in real-world passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) settings. We introduce MetaPerch, a new foundation model that achieves strong species identification performance across multiple challenging domains and present an extensive empirical study of the effects of 9 diverse metadata sources on 17 bioacoustic datasets.
